english: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that $f'(x)=\dfrac{3x^{4}-2}{x^{2}}$ for all $x\neq0$. Suppose that $f(1)=7$ and $f(x)+f(-x)=4$ for all $x\neq0$. Then the value of $f(-2)$ is ______.
hindi: माना कि $f:\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{R}$ एक अवकलनीय फलन है जिसके लिए सभी $x\neq0$ के लिए $f'(x)=\dfrac{3x^{4}-2}{x^{2}}$ है। माना कि $f(1)=7$ तथा सभी $x\neq0$ के लिए $f(x)+f(-x)=4$ है। तब $f(-2)$ का मान ______ है।
solution: $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ is two intervals, so the general solution has one constant on each: $f(x)=x^{3}+\dfrac2x+C_{1}$ ($x>0$), $f(x)=x^{3}+\dfrac2x+C_{2}$ ($x<0$)
$f(-2)=-8-1+0=-9$ (a single constant $C=4$ would give $f(x)+f(-x)=8$, which violates the condition)
solution_full: Split the integrand: $f'(x)=\dfrac{3x^{4}-2}{x^{2}}=3x^{2}-2x^{-2}$. By the power rule an antiderivative is $x^{3}+\dfrac{2}{x}$.

The domain $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ is the union of the two intervals $(-\infty,0)$ and $(0,\infty)$. On each interval two antiderivatives differ by a constant, but the constants on the two intervals are independent. So the general solution of $y'=3x^{2}-\dfrac{2}{x^{2}}$ on this domain is
For $x>0$: $f(-x)=-x^{3}-\dfrac2x+C_{2}$, so $f(x)+f(-x)=C_{1}+C_{2}$ for every $x$. The condition gives $C_{1}+C_{2}=4$, so $C_{2}=0$.
Verification: $f(x)=x^{3}+\dfrac2x+4$ ($x>0$), $f(x)=x^{3}+\dfrac2x$ ($x<0$) satisfies the differential equation on both intervals, $f(1)=7$, and $f(x)+f(-x)=4$.
Using one constant for the whole domain would force $2C=4$ and $C=4$ at the same time, a contradiction, which shows why two constants are needed.
originality_note: New: the particular solution lives on a domain made of two intervals, so the general solution carries two independent constants, and a symmetry condition f(x) + f(-x) = 4 ties them together (way 4). Closest known: finding f from f' and one value. Different because: a single-constant answer is inconsistent with the data, and the solver must recognise the two-constant general solution.
key_step: Recognising that on R minus {0} the general antiderivative has a separate constant on each side, then using the symmetry condition to link them.
justification: The integration itself is basic, but the key idea (independent constants on disjoint intervals, verified against the condition) is rarely practised, and the numerical format gives no check. Comparable to 2024-P2-Q13 (L3) where piecewise antiderivative behaviour decides the answer.
